==Problem==

A chess king is said to attack all the squares one step away from it, horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. For instance, a king on the center square of a <imath>3</imath> x <imath>3</imath> grid attacks all <imath>8</imath> other squares, as shown below. Suppose a white king and a black king are placed on different squares of a <imath>3</imath> x <imath>3</imath> grid so that they do not attack each other (in other words, not right next to each other). In how many ways can this be done?

<asy>
unitsize(29pt);
import math;
add(grid(3,3));

pair [] a = {(0.5,0.5), (0.5, 1.5), (0.5, 2.5), (1.5, 2.5), (2.5,2.5), (2.5,1.5), (2.5,0.5), (1.5,0.5)};

for (int i=0; i<a.length; ++i) {
    pair x = (1.5,1.5) + 0.4*dir(225-45*i);
    draw(x -- a[i], arrow=EndArrow());
}

label("$K$", (1.5,1.5));
</asy>

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 20 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 24 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 27 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 28 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 32</imath>


==Solution 1==

If you place a king in any of the <imath>4</imath> corners, the other king will have <imath>5</imath> spots to go and there are <imath>4</imath> corners, so <imath>5 \times 4=20</imath>.
If you place a king in any of the <imath>4</imath> edges, the other king will have <imath>3</imath> spots to go and there are <imath>4</imath> edges so <imath>3 \times 4=12</imath>. 
That gives us <imath>20+12=32</imath> spots for the other king to go into in total.
So <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)} 32}</imath> is the answer.
~andliu766, captaindiamond868 (minor edits)
~AliceDubbleYou

==Solution 2==

We see that the center is not a viable spot for either of the kings to be in, as it would attack all nearby squares.

This gives three combinations: 

Corner-corner: There are 4 corners, and none of them are touching orthogonally or diagonally, so it's <imath>\binom{4}{2}=6</imath>

Corner-edge: For each corner, there are two edges that don't border it, <imath>4\cdot2=8</imath> 

Edge-edge: The only possible combinations of this that work are top-bottom and left-right edges, so <imath>2</imath> for this type


<imath>6+8+2=16</imath> 

==Solution 3 (Complementary Counting)==

We see that the center is off-limits for the kings. Additionally, the kings cannot be next to each other. There are <imath>24</imath> ways for the kings to be placed adjacently: <imath>16</imath> corner-edge permutations and <imath>8</imath> edge-edge permutations. In total, there are <imath>8P2=56</imath> ways to arrange the kings conditions aside. Therefore, our answer is <imath>56-24=</imath><imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)} 32}</imath>

~abirgh
